title: Biophilic Design in Architecture and Its Contributions to Health, Well-being, and Sustainability: A Critical Review
central_proposition: Biophilic design serves as a theoretical framework to conceptualize 'nature' in architecture, contributing to health, well-being, and sustainability through diverse design strategies that satisfy humans' innate affiliation with nature.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilia
concept_definitions.definition: The innate tendency to focus on life and lifelike processes, representing the innately emotional affiliation of human beings to other living organisms, conserved after humankind migrated from primitive natural environments.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilic design
concept_definitions.definition: A deliberate attempt to satisfy the need of contact with natural systems and processes in the contemporary built environment, aiming to improve people's physical and mental health, productivity, and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Sustainable development
concept_definitions.definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, as brought to public attention by the Brundtland Report (UN, 1987).

concept_definitions.name: Nature-based solutions
concept_definitions.definition: Actions inspired by, supported by, or copied from nature to deploy various natural features and complex system processes in a resource-efficient way to diverse urban areas.

argument_structure: The paper traces the historical interrelation of 'nature' and architecture, reviews the emergence of biophilic design from environmental psychology theories, defines biophilic design, analyzes its contributions to sustainable architecture via the UN Sustainable Development Goals, proposes an optimized biophilic design framework with strategies and examples, and concludes with lessons learned and future research directions.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism posits that humans possess an innate, evolutionary-rooted affiliation with nature (biophilia). Biophilic design, by integrating diverse forms of 'nature' (physical, sensory, metaphorical, morphological, material, spiritual) into the built environment, satisfies this innate need. This satisfaction, in turn, elicits various psychological (e.g., stress reduction, attention restoration, positive emotions, sense of place) and physiological (e.g., healing, improved cognitive function) benefits. These human-centric benefits, combined with environmental advantages (e.g., energy reduction, biodiversity enhancement, water management), collectively contribute to broader sustainability goals.

findings.consequent: Seeking connections with nature for 'personal identity'
findings.mechanism: The dependence on nature for survival in primitive times was retained and evolved into seeking connections with nature for 'personal identity' after humans moved to modern artificial environments.
findings.quote: the 'evolutionary dependence on nature' for 'survival and personal fulfillment' forms the basis of biophilia

findings.antecedent: Contact with natural features (e.g., vegetations and water)
findings.consequent: Positive psychological reaction
findings.mechanism: Natural features generate a quick and positive psychological reaction, reducing negative emotions and fostering recovery from physiological stress and health problems.
findings.quote: Stress recovery theory proposes that contact with natural features (e.g. vegetations and water) can generate a quick and positive psychological reaction.

findings.consequent: Restored attention and reduced mental stress/brain fatigue
findings.mechanism: Cognitive tasks' excessive consumption of human attention leads to brain fatigue; interaction with nature requires less attention, providing opportunities to restore exhausted attention.
findings.quote: attention restoration theory suggests that the cognitive tasks' excessive consumption of human attention leads to brain fatigue and mental stress, and since we do not need to spend much energy on attention when interacting with nature, it can provide opportunities to restore exhausted attention

findings.antecedent: Incorporating regional natural features (e.g., geomorphology and landscape) in buildings
findings.consequent: Sense of place and sense of community, personal identity, belonging, and cohesion
findings.mechanism: Place attachment theory argues that people tend to stay in more familiar places, and connecting to the local natural environment generates a sense of place and community.
findings.quote: connecting to the local natural environment by incorporating regional features (e.g. geomorphology and landscape) in buildings could generate the 'sense of place' and 'sense of community', thereby realising personal identity, belonging, and cohesion

findings.consequent: Improved physical and mental health, productivity, and well-being
findings.mechanism: Biophilic design is a deliberate attempt to satisfy the innate human need for contact with natural systems and processes in the built environment.
findings.quote: Kellert (2008b, p.3), as one of the pioneers of biophilic design, defines it as 'a deliberate attempt to satisfy the need of contact with natural systems and processes in the contemporary built environment, and to improve people's physical and mental health, productivity and wellbeing'.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The size of water features, humidity levels, noise levels, air ventilation rates, CO2 levels, temperatures, daylight factors, daylight autonomy, plant and animal species numbers, accessible green space area/rate, viewable green space area/rate, tree canopy scale, indoor plant size/density, natural material type/quantity, color brightness/contrast, focal lengths in prospect, and fractal dimension in complexity can be quantitatively measured to evaluate biophilic design performance.
Larger-scale and higher-volume three-dimensional green spaces will demonstrate a greater positive impact on building performance and quality compared to single or isolated plants.
Quantifying the correlation between the quantity and quality of biophilic elements will reveal insights into the effectiveness of complex design typologies.
Specific biophilic design strategies, when implemented with interdisciplinary knowledge and aligned with design goals, will elicit measurable physical and psychological reactions in occupants.
Quantified exposure time to nature (e.g., 120 minutes per week in urban green spaces, 40-second views of green roofs) will correlate with measurable improvements in health and well-being.
Defining and testing optimal parameters for prospect and refuge (e.g., focal lengths ≥ 6m, preferably 30m, partition heights < 107cm) will lead to enhanced comfort and safety perceptions.
Specific fractal dimensions (e.g., 1.3-1.5 for comfort, 1.5-1.7 for interest) in architectural patterns will result in differential effects on visual interest and aesthetic preference.
bridge_warrants: Biophilic design elements can be conceptualized and developed as nature-based solutions, offering co-benefits for enhancing human health, well-being, and combating climate change.
Biophilic design provides a comprehensive framework to understand and integrate 'nature' in architecture, moving beyond superficial 'greening' to address core sustainability challenges.

The benefits of biophilic design directly and indirectly contribute to achieving multiple UN Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those related to health, well-being, energy, climate action, and biodiversity.
methodological_critiques: Existing biophilic design taxonomies suffer from uncertainties, controversies, overlaps, and vague terminology, hindering clear conceptualization and application.
Previous research often generalizes biophilic design impacts without linking them to specific effective elements, obscuring the diversity of approaches.
Quantitative evaluation of biophilic architecture is challenging due to the subjective nature of many factors and a lack of established quantitative studies and metrics.

The negative aspects and potential risks of incorporating nature into buildings (e.g., structural issues, humidity, pests, high maintenance for artificial designs) are rarely discussed in existing literature.
Biophilic design currently lacks explicit design strategies and guidelines that translate theoretical approaches and elements into concrete architectural design practices.
Architectural subfields such as materiality, tectonics, mechanical systems, and mobility are rarely linked in biophilic design studies, limiting interdisciplinary guideline development.
The effectiveness of biophilic design, especially for unmeasurable benefits, requires further validation through qualitative and quantitative research beyond promising ideas.
model_structure: The paper proposes an optimized biophilic design framework structured around three essential design approaches: Nature Incorporation, Nature Inspiration, and Nature Interaction. These approaches encompass eighteen key elements: Water, Air, Daylight, Plants, Animals, Landscape, Weather, Time and Seasonal Changes, Forms and Shapes, Patterns and Geometries, Mechanisms, Images, Materials, Texture, and Colour, Prospect and Refuge, Complexity and Order, Enticement (Peril and Mystery), Connection to Place, and Connection of Spaces. The framework aims to provide a more tangible and comprehensive understanding of biophilic design for architects.
limitations: The proposed biophilic design framework is a preliminary interpretation requiring further transformation into practical architectural design, including considerations of form, typology, scale, proportion, tectonics, and technology.
Not all forms of 'nature' are beneficial to humans; some can evoke 'biophobia' (e.g., fear of snakes, spiders, deep water).
Artificial water features may increase energy consumption, and high-volume/large-turbulence water can negatively affect acoustic quality and humidity.
Natural ventilation can increase the circulation of pollutants (e.g., PM2.5) and, with high outdoor humidity, increase the risk of mold contamination.
Glares, spilling light, and intense dynamic lighting can interfere with visual performance, be distracting, and decrease building performance.
Integrating plants can cause structural problems, excessive humidity, insect issues, odor problems, and highly artificial designs require intensive energy and maintenance.
Contact with specific animals (e.g., snakes, spiders) or the sight of dead animals can cause negative (biophobic) emotions.
Contrived superficial landscape decorations, isolated/exotic plant configurations, lack of participation/immersion, and inappropriate viewing distances/heights have limited positive impacts.
Extreme weather conditions and climate change are not beneficial to human health and comfort.
Building envelopes may be damaged or become dilapidated over time, and the perception of seasonal changes depends on individual preferences, leading to instability in visual effects of plants.
Overuse and repetition of forms and shapes can cause visual boredom.
Complex architectural shapes often require higher budgets and may cause chaos/disorder, making residents uncomfortable.
Inevitable human error in mimicking nature may lead to unbalanced systems, endangering the larger ecosystem, and a focus on external form imitation may neglect economy and feasibility in biomimicry.
Images of nature may be less effective than real natural scenes, produce undesirable effects (barren, themeless), or be influenced by personal preference.

The effectiveness of green color design in real environments is uncertain; excessively bright/high-contrast colors can produce pressure effects, and some colors (e.g., rotting brown) generate negative associations.
Disputes exist regarding the use of unprocessed, crafted, and synthetic natural materials.
The balance between prospect and refuge is difficult to define, and view qualities are highly dependent on surrounding environments.
Boredom may be caused by repeated fractal geometry, and there is a lack of consensus on the quality of visual/experiential richness and complexity.
Experiences of peril carry risks of physical injury and can lead to psychological discomfort; they are not applicable to all users/locations and increase maintenance costs in landscaped gardens.
Misunderstanding of culture and context can lead to inappropriate information or abuse, and a sense of loss may be evoked if designs change negatively or are demolished.
Single-function paths can create monotony and boredom in connection of spaces.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems.
Exposure to natural environments, including biophilic design elements, can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue.
Interactions with natural environments, facilitated by biophilic design, can lead to physiological and psychological stress reduction.
